concepts.title: Microscope Magnification and Its Many Forms
concepts.definition: A compound microscope multiplies the objective's power by the eyepiece's power - a 10x eyepiece with the 100x oil objective yields a thousand-fold view - while resolving power names the closest pair of points still seen as two; variants then bend light differently: dark field blocks central rays, phase contrast converts density into contrast, fluorophore stains glow in fluorescence microscopy, electron beams shortened a hundred thousand-fold give transmission and scanning modes, and confocal optics sharpen labelled fixed cells.
concepts.key_idea: Multiply objective by eyepiece for total magnification; pick the microscopy variant by what must be seen - surfaces, organelles or glowing probes.
question_patterns: a student microscope carries a 15x eyepiece and a 45x objective - compute the total magnification
which combination of the 4x 10x 40x and 100x objectives with a 10x eyepiece gives 400x
differentiate transmission from scanning electron microscopy on the basis of how the image forms
why does phase contrast microscopy suit organelles and chromosomes without staining
how many times shorter is the electron beam wavelength than visible light
which microscopy form identifies bacteria or viruses in immunodiagnosis and why
what can resolving power measure that magnification alone cannot

solution_steps.explain: The objective magnifies first and the eyepiece enlarges that image again.
Multiply the real size by the total power for the apparent size.

worked_examples.q: A 10x eyepiece with the 100x oil objective gives what total magnification?

concepts.title: Centrifugation and Its Types
concepts.definition: Spinning samples around an axis lets centrifugal force sort particles by density: differential centrifugation exploits differing sedimentation rates to drop nuclei, mitochondria or chloroplasts in turn, density-gradient runs settle molecules at levels matching their densities inside a preformed gradient, and ultracentrifugation pushes past one hundred thousand times gravity to separate dissolved molecules.
concepts.key_idea: Rate of sedimentation sorts by size and density in differential runs; a gradient sorts similar-sized particles purely by density.
question_patterns: differentiate differential density-gradient and ultracentrifugation with one application of each
at what minimum relative centrifugal force does ultracentrifugation begin
which centrifuge type would first pellet nuclei and then mitochondria from a cell extract
why do heavier molecules travel outward faster in a density gradient
name the three commonly used centrifuge instruments in a laboratory
what does rpm measure in a spinning centrifuge rotor

solution_steps.explain: Whole organelles call for differential runs; similar-sized particles call for gradients; dissolved molecules need ultracentrifugation.
Speeds at or above 100,000 x g define ultracentrifugation.
Pellets form at tube bottoms in differential runs; bands sit at their density levels in gradients.

worked_examples.q: Which centrifugation exploits differing sedimentation rates: differential or density-gradient?

concepts.title: Electrophoresis of DNA and Proteins
concepts.definition: An electric field walks charged macromolecules through a gel at speeds set by their charge-to-size ratio: negatively charged DNA threads from the wells toward the anode with short pieces outrunning long ones across an 80-120 volt run, while SDS coats proteins uniformly negative so polyacrylamide gels - loose at 4-8 percent for big proteins, hard at 12-20 percent for small ones - resolve them, with bromophenol blue racing ahead as the tracking dye and ethidium bromide or Coomassie blue making the bands visible.
concepts.key_idea: DNA sorts by size alone toward the anode; SDS-PAGE sorts proteins by size after the detergent equalises their charge.
question_patterns: why do shorter DNA fragments migrate faster than longer ones in agarose gel electrophoresis
toward which electrode does DNA move and which phosphate-bearing feature gives it that charge
which voltage range runs a standard agarose DNA gel
a 4 percent and a 12 percent polyacrylamide gel are prepared - which resolves low molecular weight proteins and why
what roles do the tracking dye and the DNA ladder play in a gel run
why must ethidium bromide be handled with great care and how does it reveal DNA under UV
who first observed electrophoretic migration and in which year

solution_steps.explain: Agarose gels suit nucleic acids; polyacrylamide with crosslinker suits proteins.
SDS wraps proteins in uniform negative charge so separation follows size.
EtBr fluoresces under UV for DNA; Coomassie stains protein bands blue; the dye front signals when to stop.

worked_examples.q: Negatively charged DNA migrates toward which electrode: the anode or the cathode?

concepts.title: ELISA Formats for Antigen and Antibody
concepts.definition: Engvall and Perlman's 1971 enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay quantifies antigen or antibody through an enzyme's colour signal: direct ELISA coats antigen and adds one labelled antibody; indirect adds an unlabelled primary then a labelled secondary for extra sensitivity; sandwich traps antigen between a captured and a second labelled antibody for high specificity; and competitive ELISA reads antigen amounts inversely, more antigen meaning weaker colour.
concepts.key_idea: Count the antibodies and which one carries the enzyme - that tells you the format and what the colour measures.
question_patterns: differentiate direct indirect sandwich and competitive ELISA with the antibodies used in each
in competitive ELISA why does a higher antigen concentration give a weaker colour
which ELISA format needs no secondary antibody and which gains sensitivity from multiple labelled secondaries
what is an epitope and why does sandwich ELISA use antibodies to two different epitopes
who invented ELISA and in which year
name three applications of ELISA in diagnosis and the food industry

solution_steps.explain: Antigen-coated wells suit direct and indirect; antibody-coated wells suit sandwich; antigen-coated with pre-incubation signals competitive.
Direct uses one enzyme-conjugated antibody; indirect and sandwich add a labelled secondary; competitive measures what failed to bind.
Substrate turnover measured by an ELISA reader converts colour intensity into concentration via a standard curve.

worked_examples.q: Which ELISA traps antigen between two antibodies: sandwich or direct?

concepts.title: Chromatography Modes from Adsorption to Gas
concepts.definition: Chromatography races solutes between a moving eluent and a held stationary phase, each molecule eluting in step with its affinity: adsorption onto polar surfaces, partitioning between immiscible solvents, ion-exchange electrostatics, molecular sieving in gel filtration, biospecific ligand capture in affinity columns, high-pressure liquid runs through fine particles, and gas chromatography for volatiles - all traced as peaks on a chromatogram.
concepts.key_idea: Name the mode by what holds the solute back - surface, solvent, charge, pore, ligand, pressure or volatility.
question_patterns: match adsorption partition ion-exchange gel filtration affinity HPLC and gas chromatography with the principle each exploits
what is a chromatogram and what do its peaks represent
which chromatography mode purifies a protein through the binding specificity of an immobilised ligand
how does gel filtration separate molecules - on what property of the solute
why must the mobile phase be pumped under high pressure in HPLC
which chromatography suits volatile alcohols and ketones and which suits antibiotic fractionation

solution_steps.explain: Silica, resin, gel beads, ligand or fine particles reveal the separation principle.
Weakly held solutes elute first; size, charge or affinity decides the rest.
Collected fractions and chromatogram peaks report the separation.

worked_examples.q: Which chromatography uses biospecific ligand capture: affinity or gas?

concepts.title: Beer-Lambert Law Quantitation
concepts.definition: Light lost equals solute present: the Beer-Lambert law writes absorbance as the molar absorptivity times path length times concentration, with transmittance as the ratio of transmitted to incident intensity, so a colorimeter with its filters or a spectrophotometer with its prism turns any coloured solution into a number - and the same spectroscopy family, from infrared to NMR and mass spectrometry, identifies functional groups, metals and molecular structures.
concepts.key_idea: Divide the measured absorbance by absorptivity times path length to recover the concentration; transmittance is simply transmitted over incident.
question_patterns: a solution reads absorbance 0.45 in a 1 cm cuvette with molar absorptivity 900 - compute its concentration
state the Beer-Lambert law defining each symbol in the equation
incident light of 100 units falls on a sample and 25 units emerge - find the transmittance
how does a spectrophotometer select one wavelength while a colorimeter uses a filter bandwidth
list the components of a spectrophotometer from source to digital display
which spectroscopic technique detects trace metals and which reveals atomic chemical environments

solution_steps.explain: Rearranging absorbance equals absorptivity times path times concentration gives the concentration.
Transmittance divides the emerging intensity by the incident one.

worked_examples.q: In the Beer-Lambert law, absorbance equals absorptivity times path length times what: concentration or colour?

concepts.title: Automated DNA Sequencing Speed
concepts.definition: Sanger's chain-termination chemistry - ddNTPs lacking the 3-prime hydroxyl stopping each growing strand, four tubes then a PAGE read bottom-up - became the gold standard, while Maxam-Gilbert cleaved bases chemically; automation replaced radioactivity with four fluorescent rhodamine ddNTPs in one capillary tube, so a task needing a person's whole year of manual work, twenty to fifty thousand bases, now finishes in a few hours at roughly half the material cost.
concepts.key_idea: Divide the year's hours by the automated run's hours to price the speed-up that fluorescent automation delivered.
question_patterns: manual sequencing yields 40000 bases per person-year while an automated sequencer needs only 4 hours for the same - compute the fold speed-up
why does a dideoxynucleotide terminate chain growth - name the missing group
what goes into each of the four tubes of a classic Sanger reaction and what ends every fragment in a lane
differentiate the Sanger method from the Maxam-Gilbert chemical degradation method
which four fluorescent dyes label the four ddNTPs in automated sequencing
how does next-generation sequencing differ from Sanger sequencing in scale and validation use
in which order is a Sanger gel read on the X-ray film

solution_steps.explain: Divide the yearly base output by the hours in a year.
Dividing the year's hours by the automated hours gives the fold speed-up.

worked_examples.q: Sanger's chain termination lacks which group to stop strands: the 3-prime hydroxyl or the base?

concepts.title: FISH, Microarray and Flow Cytometry Profiling
concepts.definition: Three probes-on-cells techniques close the toolkit: fluorescent in situ hybridisation anneals a labelled DNA probe to its chromosome site and even paints every chromosome a different colour; DNA microarrays hybridise Cy3/Cy5-labelled cDNA onto thousands of immobilised probes to flag upregulated and downregulated genes; and flow cytometry streams single cells past lasers - a Coulter-counter idea from the late 1950s - reading scattered and fluorescent light to count and sort labelled populations.
concepts.key_idea: Label the probe or the cell, let complementarity or a laser do the sorting, and read the colours as biology.
question_patterns: list the main steps of a FISH experiment from probe design to fluorescent microscopy
how does chromosome painting assign a unique colour to every chromosome
arrange the four steps of a DNA microarray experiment in order
why are upregulated genes shown green and downregulated red on a microarray scan
which dyes commonly label cDNA for microarray hybridisation
explain the principle of flow cytometry from the Coulter counter to laser-based sorting
which technique quantifies expression of thousands of genes in parallel and which locates a gene on its chromosome

solution_steps.explain: Design a complementary, fluorescently labelled molecule - FISH probe or cDNA fragment.
Anneal to denatured chromosomes or array spots; in cytometry, stream single cells past the laser.
Fluorescent spots map genes, colour ratios report expression, and scatter plus fluorescence classify each cell.

worked_examples.q: Which technique anneals a labelled DNA probe to its chromosome site: FISH or flow cytometry?
